stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Materials scientists have generally treated graphene as a filler whose benefits scale with quantity: the more flakes mixed into a polymer, the stiffer the resulting composite. A 2025 study by Ana Oduya's team suggests that picture is incomplete. In epoxy samples, stiffness rose steadily up to about 1 percent graphene by weight, then flattened and even dipped as the flakes clumped into stacks that slid past one another. When the team coated the flakes with a surfactant that kept them separated, however, stiffness continued to climb through 3 percent. What limits the composite, the results imply, is less how much graphene it holds than how evenly that graphene is spread.
choices: To present a coating method that allows epoxy composites to hold larger amounts of graphene without clumping
To argue that graphene stops being useful as a stiffening filler once it exceeds about 1 percent by weight
To qualify a common assumption about graphene fillers by showing that dispersion, not quantity alone, governs stiffness
To support a common assumption about graphene fillers by showing that added flakes keep increasing a composite's stiffness
explanation: The text opens with a belief (stiffness rises with the amount of graphene) and immediately signals doubt: 'that picture is incomplete.' The uncoated samples show that the belief fails once flakes clump. The coated samples show that graphene still works when the flakes stay separated. The final sentence draws the conclusion: how evenly the graphene is spread matters more than how much there is. So the text qualifies the common view. It doesn't throw it out. It names dispersion as the condition the view left out.

A.why: You picked something the text contains, not what it is for. The surfactant coating is evidence, not the point. The text never describes the method in any detail, and it uses the coating only to show that clumping, not graphene itself, caused the plateau.

B.why: You saw correctly that the text challenges the common view, but then you finished the thought too strongly. The coated samples kept getting stiffer through 3 percent, so the text directly contradicts the idea that graphene stops being useful above 1 percent. The text limits the belief. It doesn't reverse it.

D.why: You latched onto the coated samples, where stiffness did keep rising, and ignored the author's framing. The text calls the common picture 'incomplete,' and the uncoated samples got less stiff as more graphene was added. The text is qualifying the assumption, not supporting it.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Linguists have often assumed that writing acts as a brake on language change: once words are fixed on the page, the reasoning goes, speakers replace them more slowly. To test this, Tomasz Wierzba compared twelve pairs of closely related languages in which one member had a centuries-old literary tradition and the other had been used almost entirely in speech. Across everyday vocabulary (words for kin, body parts, and weather), the rate at which words were replaced was nearly identical within each pair. Only among terms used chiefly in legal and religious texts did the written languages show markedly slower turnover.
choices: To report that languages with long literary traditions replace their legal and religious vocabulary more slowly than spoken languages do
To suggest that the supposed slowing effect of writing on vocabulary change applies to a narrower range of words than is often assumed
To show that a long tradition of writing has no measurable effect on how quickly a language replaces the words it uses
To explain why everyday words such as kin terms resist replacement more strongly than specialized legal and religious terms do
explanation: The text opens with what linguists 'have often assumed': writing slows vocabulary change. The study then tests that belief. For everyday words, writing made no difference. Only legal and religious terms changed more slowly in the written languages. The author never states a conclusion, so you have to infer it: writing's slowing effect is real but much narrower than the broad assumption claims. That makes the text's purpose to narrow the belief, which is what B says.

A.why: This accurately restates the final sentence, which is why it's tempting. But it describes one finding, not the job the text does. The text exists to test a belief about writing in general, and you can only see that by reading the first sentence along with the last.

C.why: You noticed that the everyday-vocabulary result undercuts the assumption, then stopped reading too soon. The final sentence reports that writing did slow turnover in legal and religious terms, so 'no measurable effect' is contradicted. The text limits the claim. It doesn't disprove it.

D.why: You mixed up the comparison. The study compares written languages with spoken ones. It doesn't compare everyday words with specialized words in terms of how well they resist change. Within the written languages, it was the legal and religious terms that changed more slowly, not the everyday ones. The text also offers no explanation of why.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Ornithologists have often explained the dawn chorus, the burst of birdsong near sunrise, by pointing to the air. Cool, still mornings let sound travel farther, so singing then supposedly reaches more rivals and mates. Ecologist Ines Varga's recordings in Hungarian woodlands confirm that songs do carry about 20 percent farther at dawn than at noon. Yet on overcast days when those still conditions lasted until midday, the birds did not sing for longer; the chorus ended on schedule. The acoustic edge, Varga concludes, is a benefit birds collect, not the reason they sing when they do.
choices: To present measurements showing that birdsong travels farther in the cool, still air of early morning
To argue that a real acoustic advantage of dawn singing does not explain why birds sing at that hour
To show that the still morning air credited with carrying birdsong has little effect on how far it travels
To suggest that birds shift the timing of their singing to whichever conditions offer the best acoustics
explanation: The text opens with a belief: birds sing at dawn because sound carries farther then. Varga confirms the advantage is real, but the overcast-day finding shows that the birds' timing doesn't follow it. So the text keeps the fact and rejects it as the explanation. Choice B gets both halves.

A.why: You picked what the text contains, not what it's for. The measurements are one step. They're there to concede the acoustic advantage before the text shows it doesn't explain the timing.

C.why: You saw that the belief gets challenged and assumed the challenge targets the acoustic fact. Varga's recordings confirm that songs carry about 20 percent farther at dawn. What she challenges is the explanation, not the fact.

D.why: This is the opposite of the finding. When still conditions lasted until midday, the birds kept their usual timing and did not sing longer.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Many agronomists have credited no-till farming, which means planting without plowing, with locking carbon from the air into the soil. Most supporting studies, however, sampled only the top 30 centimeters. Soil scientist Ruth Adeyemi's team sampled to a full meter on forty paired farms. No-till fields held more carbon near the surface, but plowed fields held more below it, and the totals were nearly identical. Adeyemi stresses that no-till still curbs erosion. What the deeper samples undercut is the claim that it adds stored carbon.
choices: To argue that no-till farming offers no meaningful environmental advantage over conventional plowing
To explain how plowing redistributes carbon from the soil surface into the deeper layers below it
To show that shallow sampling has led researchers to underestimate the carbon held in no-till fields
To question whether a widely credited benefit of no-till farming survives a more complete measurement
explanation: The belief is that no-till farming stores extra carbon. 'However' signals doubt. The one-meter samples show equal totals, so the earlier result came from sampling only the surface. The last sentence narrows the challenge to the carbon claim alone, and Choice D matches that scope.

A.why: You read the challenge as a rejection. Adeyemi says outright that no-till still curbs erosion. Only the carbon benefit is in doubt.

B.why: This is the content trap. Where carbon sits in plowed fields is evidence inside the study. The text uses it to question a belief, not to teach how plowing works.

C.why: You spotted that sampling depth matters but reversed the direction. Shallow samples made no-till look better, because its carbon sits near the surface. They overstated its stored carbon.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Icelandic is often cited as proof that isolation slows language change, since modern Icelanders can read medieval sagas with little difficulty. Linguist Tomas Brekke points out that this ease of reading reflects stable grammar and spelling, which Icelandic has indeed preserved. Its sound system tells another story. Several vowels have shifted so far since the sagas were written that a medieval speaker would likely struggle to follow a modern one. Isolation, Brekke argues, may have preserved some parts of the language while leaving others free to change.
choices: To complicate a familiar example of linguistic stability by showing that it holds only for certain features
To argue that geographic isolation has had no real effect on how the Icelandic language has developed
To describe how the pronunciation of several Icelandic vowels has shifted since medieval times
To explain why modern Icelanders can read medieval sagas despite major changes in grammar
explanation: The text opens with Icelandic as the standard example of a language that stays stable when it's isolated. Brekke grants that grammar and spelling are stable, then shows that the sound system changed a lot. His conclusion is that stability covers only some features. Choice A says the example is complicated, not thrown out.

B.why: You took the challenge further than Brekke does. He says isolation 'may have preserved some parts' of Icelandic, so it does have an effect, just an uneven one.

C.why: This is accurate but it's the content trap. The vowel shifts are the evidence. The text is for questioning what Icelandic proves, not for cataloging sound changes.

D.why: The text says grammar has stayed stable, not that it changed a lot. Reading is easy because the grammar didn't change.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: News reports often treat falling antibody levels after vaccination as a sign that protection is vanishing. Antibodies are the easiest part of the immune response to measure, so their decline months after a shot is simple to chart. But immunologist Priya Nandakumar's team tracked vaccinated adults whose antibodies had dropped sharply and found that their memory B cells and T cells remained abundant. These individuals caught mild infections more often than before, yet they were rarely hospitalized. A shrinking antibody count, the team concludes, captures only part of what a vaccine leaves behind.
choices: To argue that falling antibody levels reveal nothing about how well a vaccine still protects people
To describe how memory B cells and T cells respond when a vaccinated person encounters a virus
To caution that declining antibody counts may overstate how much protection a vaccine has lost
To show that antibody levels after vaccination stay steadier than many news reports have suggested
explanation: The belief comes first: falling antibodies mean vanishing protection. 'But' starts the evidence against it. Memory cells stay abundant and severe illness stays rare. Mild infections did rise, though, so some protection was lost. The text warns against overstating the loss rather than denying it. Choice C keeps that limit.

A.why: This is the second trap. You caught the challenge but finished it too strongly. Mild infections rose as antibodies fell, so antibody levels do tell you something. The team says they show 'only part' of the picture.

B.why: You described what the study looked at, not what the text is for. The memory-cell finding is evidence against the opening belief.

D.why: The text agrees that antibodies drop sharply. It challenges what the drop means, not whether it happens.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: For decades, metallurgists have relied on a simple rule: the smaller the crystal grains in a metal, the stronger it is, because the boundaries between grains block the defects that let metal deform. Engineers have exploited this by refining grains ever further. In tests on copper, however, materials scientist Kenji Mori found that strength rose only until grains shrank to about 15 nanometers. Below that size, samples grew weaker. At such scales, Mori suggests, boundaries become so numerous that grains begin sliding past one another along them.
choices: To argue that refining grain size is an unreliable way to strengthen metals such as copper
To show that copper grows steadily weaker as its crystal grains are made smaller and smaller
To identify a limit on a long-trusted rule by showing that it breaks down below a certain grain size
To explain how grain boundaries allow neighboring crystal grains to slide past one another
explanation: The text states a long-trusted rule, then 'however' brings in Mori's result. Strength rises as grains shrink until about 15 nanometers, then falls. The rule holds over a range and fails past a threshold. Choice C says the rule has a limit, not that it's wrong.

A.why: You treated a limit as a rejection. Mori's copper got stronger as grains shrank, right down to about 15 nanometers. Refining grains works until that point.

B.why: You read only the second half of the finding. Strength rose first and fell only below about 15 nanometers, so it didn't decline steadily.

D.why: This is the content trap. The sliding mechanism is Mori's suggested cause, in the last sentence. The text is for limiting the rule, not for explaining the mechanism.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: City officials have long assumed that diets in low-income neighborhoods suffer mainly because fresh food is hard to reach, so a full-service grocery store should improve what residents eat. Economist Dana Whitlock followed households before and after such a store opened in one district, and many residents did switch to shopping there. Their purchases, however, changed little: spending on fruit and vegetables barely rose. Whitlock notes that access matters, but price and long-standing habits appear to matter at least as much.
choices: To challenge the view that limited access is the chief reason some neighborhoods' diets suffer
To argue that access to fresh food has no bearing on what residents of poorer neighborhoods eat
To show that residents of the district avoided the new grocery store because of its high prices
To describe how one district's households changed their shopping after a grocery store opened
explanation: The belief is that poor diets come mainly from limited access. 'However' introduces the evidence: residents used the new store, but their purchases barely changed. Whitlock's conclusion keeps access as a factor while denying it's the main one. Choice A challenges exactly that word 'mainly'.

B.why: You saw the challenge and pushed it to total rejection. Whitlock says plainly that 'access matters'.

C.why: Many residents did switch to the new store. Price is offered as a reason their purchases didn't change, not as a reason they stayed away.

D.why: This is the content trap. Most of the text is about the study, but the study is there as evidence against the officials' assumption.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Coaches now commonly warn athletes against static stretching, holding a muscle at full length, before competition. They cite studies in which stretching reduced sprint speed and jump height. Sports scientist Leah Okafor reexamined those studies and noticed that most had participants hold each stretch for a minute or more, often with no other warm-up. In her own trials, sprinters held stretches for 20 to 30 seconds, as athletes typically do, and then did a dynamic warm-up. They ran no slower than sprinters who skipped stretching altogether.
choices: To argue that static stretching improves sprinters' speed as long as each stretch is kept brief
To show that the studies linking stretching to slower sprints used holds too short to matter
To compare how static stretches and dynamic warm-ups each affect sprinters' running times
To suggest that a warning against stretching rests on conditions athletes rarely reproduce
explanation: The belief here is the coaches' warning against stretching. Okafor shows that the evidence for it used unusually long holds with no warm-up. Under normal conditions she found no slowdown. The text questions the warning's basis but doesn't claim stretching helps. Choice D stays within what the text shows.

A.why: You flipped the warning into its opposite. Okafor's stretchers ran 'no slower', which is not the same as faster. The text never says stretching improves speed.

B.why: You got the direction backward. The earlier studies used holds that were longer than usual, a minute or more, not shorter.

C.why: The text never compares static stretching with dynamic warm-ups. Both groups' conditions are details of Okafor's trial, which is there to test the coaches' warning.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Shop owners often oppose replacing street parking with bike lanes, reasoning that most of their customers arrive by car. Planner Marco Duval surveyed merchants and shoppers on two commercial streets. Merchants estimated that about half their customers drove, while the shoppers' own answers put the figure below one-fifth. Cyclists spent less per visit than drivers but came more often, so their monthly spending was similar. Duval's data do not show that bike lanes raise sales, but they suggest that merchants' fears rest on a mistaken picture of their own customers.
choices: To argue that replacing street parking with bike lanes increases sales at the shops nearby
To suggest that merchants' opposition to bike lanes reflects a misjudgment of their customers
To show that cyclists are more valuable customers than drivers because they spend more per visit
To compare how often drivers and cyclists visited shops along two commercial streets
explanation: The belief belongs to the merchants: most of our customers drive, so bike lanes will hurt us. Duval's surveys show merchants greatly overestimate the share who drive, and that cyclists spend about as much each month. The last sentence says the fear rests on a mistaken picture, and Choice B matches that.

A.why: You turned 'the fear is mistaken' into 'the change helps'. The text says Duval's data 'do not show that bike lanes raise sales'.

C.why: Cyclists spent less per visit. Their monthly spending only matched drivers' because they visited more often.

D.why: This is the content trap. How often each group visited is one piece of evidence, and it's there to challenge the merchants' belief.
